notes.meaning: Some time later, during the dry wheat harvest, Samson returned to visit his wife. He brought a young goat as a gift of peace, planning to enter her room and be reunited with her. Her father, however, stood in the doorway and refused to let him inside.

The father claimed he assumed Samson thoroughly hated the woman after leaving her, so he gave her in marriage to Samson's best man. To make amends, he offered Samson her younger and prettier sister instead. Samson turned down the offer, knowing that God's law forbade taking a wife's sister while she was living.

Samson announced that the Philistines could no longer blame him for whatever harm he was about to cause them. He had made an honest effort to restore his marriage, but their unfair actions gave him a clear reason to strike back. As a leader in Israel, he used this personal injury to start weakening the nation that oppressed his people.

Samson went out and captured three hundred foxes or wild jackals from the countryside. He tied them in pairs by their tails and fastened a burning torch between each pair. Pairing them forced the animals to pull in opposite directions across the open fields instead of running straight to their dens.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars translate the Hebrew word as jackals rather than foxes, because jackals roamed together in large packs and were far easier to trap in great numbers.

notes.meaning: Samson lit the torches and let the animals loose among the Philistines' fields. Because the wheat was dry and ready for harvest, the fire spread rapidly through the shocks of cut grain, the standing fields, the vineyards, and the olive groves. This attack struck a devastating blow to the Philistines by destroying their main food supplies.

When the Philistines learned that Samson burned their crops because his wife had been given away, an angry mob burned both the woman and her father to death. This was a dark and tragic turn of events. Samson's wife had previously betrayed his secret to save her home from fire, yet that very doom caught up with her in the end.

Samson told the Philistines that killing the woman did not settle the matter, and he vowed not to stop until he took full vengeance on them. Even though the mob had punished the family that wronged him, he still had a larger duty to fight Israel's oppressors. He refused to lay down his anger until justice was carried out.

differ.view: Some Baptists follow John Gill in teaching that Samson acted here not out of selfish revenge, but as God's appointed judge executing public justice for Israel.
Other evangelicals see Samson as driven by personal anger and a bitter cycle of retaliation, which God still used to accomplish His sovereign purposes.

notes.meaning: Samson struck down the Philistines with great force, dealing them a crushing defeat. Afterward, he withdrew to a natural fortress in the cleft of the cliff of Etam in Judah. He retreated there alone to wait and see how the Philistines would react to the blow he had struck.

The Philistines gathered an army and marched up into the territory of Judah, setting up camp near a place called Lehi. They came in force to hunt down Samson and avenge the heavy losses he had inflicted. This military buildup was designed to intimidate the people of Judah into surrendering him.

The men of Judah asked the Philistine commanders why they had brought an army against them. The Philistines answered that they only came to arrest Samson and pay him back for what he had done. They promised not to harm the tribe of Judah as long as Samson was handed over to them.

Three thousand men of Judah went down to Samson's cave, scolding him for angering the Philistines who ruled over them. Samson replied that he had only treated the Philistines as they had treated him. The men of Judah had become comfortable under foreign rule, fearing their pagan masters far more than they trusted God's deliverer.

The men of Judah told Samson they had come to tie him up and surrender him to the Philistines. Samson agreed to surrender peacefully, but only after making them swear they would not attack him themselves. Samson had the power to fight off his own countrymen, but he chose not to shed the blood of his brothers.

The men promised they would not kill him, but they bound him securely with two brand-new ropes. Samson allowed himself to be tied and led out from the rock toward the Philistine camp. His quiet submission showed remarkable patience and trust that God would see him through the trap.

As Samson approached Lehi, the Philistines shouted with joy, thinking their greatest enemy was finally helpless in their grasp. At that moment, the Spirit of the LORD came upon Samson with overwhelming power. The sturdy ropes around his arms snapped like burnt flax and dropped from his hands like melting wax.

Finding the fresh jawbone of a dead donkey on the ground, Samson picked it up and struck down a thousand Philistine soldiers. The fresh bone was tough and did not snap under the impact of the battle. God used this crude, lowly object to show that real victory comes from His Spirit, not fine military weapons.

After the slaughter, Samson recited a victory song about how he had piled up bodies using only the jawbone of a donkey. His poem was a clever rhyme that highlighted the utter humiliation of the Philistines. Even after facing an entire army alone, he openly proclaimed the complete defeat of his foes.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Scholars note that the Hebrew line contains an intentional wordplay, as the words for donkey and heap sound identical, allowing the phrase to mean heaps upon heaps or making donkeys out of them.

notes.meaning: When Samson finished his song, he threw the jawbone away from his hand. He then named the place Ramath-lehi, which means 'Jawbone Height' or 'the casting away of the jawbone.' The new name created a lasting memorial to the victory God worked that day.

Exhausted from the fierce battle in the summer heat, Samson suffered from extreme thirst and feared he would collapse. He cried out to the LORD, giving God the credit for granting such a massive victory. He prayed that the Lord would not allow His own servant to die of thirst and fall into the hands of ungodly enemies.

God answered Samson's plea by splitting open a hollow basin in the ground at Lehi, causing fresh water to pour out. Samson drank, his physical strength returned, and his spirit was revived. He named the spring En-hakkore, meaning 'the spring of the one who called,' and it continued to flow there for years to come.

Samson led and defended Israel as a judge for twenty years while the Philistines occupied the land. Even though the Philistines remained in power, God used Samson to hold them back and protect the Israelites from destruction. His leadership proved that the Lord never abandons His people, even in their darkest seasons.
